verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them: ‘When either man or woman shall make a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to Yahweh,
he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of fermented drink, neither shall he drink any juice of grapes, nor eat fresh grapes or dried.
All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is made of the grapevine, from the seeds even to the skins.

“‘All the days of his vow of separation no razor shall come on his head, until the days are fulfilled, in which he separates himself to Yahweh. He shall be holy. He shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow long.
“‘All the days that he separates himself to Yahweh he shall not go near a dead body.
He shall not make himself unclean for his father, or for his mother, for his brother, or for his sister, when they die; because his separation to God  is on his head.
All the days of his separation he is holy to Yahweh.
“‘If any man dies very suddenly beside him, and he defiles the head of his separation; then he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing. On the seventh day he shall shave it.
On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, to the door of the Tent of Meeting.
The priest shall offer one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead, and shall make his head holy that same day.
He shall separate to Yahweh the days of his separation, and shall bring a male lamb a year old for a trespass offering; but the former days shall be void, because his separation was defiled.
“‘This is the law of the Nazirite: when the days of his separation are fulfilled, he shall be brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting,

and he shall offer his offering to Yahweh, one male lamb a year old without defect for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without defect for a sin offering, and one ram without defect for peace offerings,
and a basket of unleavened bread, cakes of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and their meal offering, and their drink offerings.
The priest shall present them before Yahweh, and shall offer his sin offering, and his burnt offering.
He shall offer the ram for a sacrifice of peace offerings to Yahweh, with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall offer also its meal offering, and its drink offering.

The Nazirite shall shave the head of his separation at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and shall take the hair of the head of his separation, and put it on the fire which is under the sacrifice of peace offerings.

The priest shall take the boiled shoulder of the ram, and one unleavened cake out of the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved the head of his separation;

and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before Yahweh. This is holy for the priest, together with the breast that is waved and the thigh that is offered. After that the Nazirite may drink wine.

“‘This is the law of the Nazirite who vows, and of his offering to Yahweh for his separation, besides that which he is able to get. According to his vow which he vows, so he must do after the law of his separation.’”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.’ You shall tell them,
‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you.
Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you.
Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
“So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.”

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks to Moses about those who wish to draw near to Him through a special vow. Sometimes the heart yearns for a deeper separation unto the Lord—and He welcomes it, not as pride, but as honest seeking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A Nazirite vow was voluntary, open to man or woman alike—a radical choice to set oneself apart for the Lord's sake. Notice: the Lord does not command it, but He honors it when the heart chooses to abandon the ordinary path for His sake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No wine, no strong drink—not because wine itself is sin, but because separation to the Lord means laying down the tastes and ease we reach for. The Nazirite chose clarity and focus over comfort, a quiet witness to a life hidden in God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the grape itself—the seed and the skin—was off limits. Such care in the law shows how seriously the Lord takes a vow made in earnest. Every small choice reinforced the separation, every day a renewal of the heart's intention.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The uncut hair of a Nazirite was a visible sign—a crown of separation worn for all to see. Long hair meant vulnerability too; in that culture, it marked someone set apart, someone whose appearance proclaimed their heart's devotion to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even contact with death itself broke the vow. Life separated to God must stay clear of what brings defilement—a hard word, but it speaks to the seriousness with which the Lord guards the consecrated heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not even grief for a parent could break the vow. The law's coldness startles us—yet it teaches that when we vow separation to God, that covenant stands above all earthly ties. The head that bears His mark is not our own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the days of separation—not just some days, not just the public ones—the Nazirite was holy to the Lord. Consecration is not a performance for others; it is a constant reality before God, whether anyone sees it or not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even a sudden death nearby could defile the vow. The law made no exception for accidents or grief—the separation was that fragile, that demanding. Yet this very fragility taught Israel: holiness requires vigilance, and our own strength cannot hold us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two doves or pigeons—the offering of the poor, the humble. Whether rich or poor came to make things right, the Lord's way was the same: bring what you can, bring it to the door of His dwelling, and seek atonement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest makes atonement for the broken vow. What the person had defiled by accident, the Lord restores through the priest's work—a picture of how grace repairs what our frailty has marred, if we bring it to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The days lost through defilement do not count; the Nazirite must begin the count anew. How like the Lord's kindness—He does not erase the vow but lets the heart start fresh, keeping the separation alive despite the stumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the vow was fulfilled, the Nazirite was brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting—the threshold of God's dwelling. The conclusion of separation was not private, but public, witnessed before the Lord and His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three animals—for burnt offering, sin offering, peace offerings—all without defect. The Nazirite's completion was costly, and the Lord's acceptance required the best the person could bring, offered with these three motions of the heart: surrender, repentance, and peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bread, oil, fine flour—the daily sustenance consecrated and offered. Even the simple gift of food became holy when brought with a true heart, part of the great action of thanksgiving for days faithfully separated to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest presented them before Yahweh—the living God sees every offering, every gesture of the consecrated heart. The priest was only the intermediary; the real witness, the real receiver, was the Lord Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The peace offering was accompanied by unleavened bread and a meal offering—symbols of readiness and purity. The Nazirite's separation culminated in an offering of peace, a renewed covenant of shalom between the devoted heart and its God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the door of the Tent of Meeting, the Nazirite shaved the head that had grown long in separation and placed those locks on the fire beneath the peace offering. The visible sign of consecration was released to the flame—a beautiful ending to the vow's outward witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The boiled shoulder, the cake, the wafer—placed on the open hands of the Nazirite. These were handed back as a gift, a sign that what the Nazirite had given was received and now returned as a blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the Nazirite could drink wine again. The vow was ended; the separation was complete; and the person returned to ordinary life—yet forever marked by the Lord, forever changed by having been set apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The law of the Nazirite was fixed: each person must do according to their own vow. Not all were called to it, yet the Lord kept the door open for any who felt the heart's pull to separate themselves wholly to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the Lord speaks again to Moses about blessing. After the law of separation comes the law of blessing—as if to say, those who draw near to God are the ones fitted to be channels of His blessing to others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron and his sons were the priests—and they were given the privilege of blessing Israel by putting the Lord's name upon them. What a trust: to speak God's name over His people and seal His care upon their lives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh bless you, and keep you—the first words of the Aaronic blessing, the prayer the priests were commanded to pray. In the Lord's blessing is both abundance and protection, provision and safety, all wrapped in one covenant word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Make His face to shine on you, and be gracious to you—I think of the way a parent's face lights up when their child enters the room. The Lord's face turned toward us in grace is the deepest assurance any heart can know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace—the final word of the Aaronic blessing, which has echoed through Israel for thousands of years and still echoes in the church today. Peace: not as the world gives, but the shalom of a face fully turned toward us in love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them. Looking back from this later road, I see how the Lord's name—spoken, taught, lived out—still marks His people today. His blessing follows the placing of His name upon us, and we carry it wherever we go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
